d01.title: Where should you actually sleep?
d01.strong: Sleep inside the core; treat a metro address as a downgrade, not a discount.
d01.rest: For a first trip of three or four days, book Centro Storico if the budget allows and Monti if it doesn’t — both put the centre thirteen minutes’ walk away. Choose Trastevere only if evenings matter more than mornings, and accept the bridge. Termini is a fine place to change trains and a poor place to wake up.

d02.title: Do you need transit tickets at all?
d02.strong: If you slept in the core, skip the pass and tap a contactless card.
d02.rest: The daily fare cap means you never overpay and never do arithmetic at a machine. Reach for the Roma Pass only if you’re genuinely transport-heavy and hitting two or more of its sights; reach for the Omnia only for a three-day Colosseum-and-Vatican blitz. Buying either “to be safe” is the easiest way to overpay in Rome.

d03.title: Train, or the fixed-fare taxi from the airport?
d03.strong: Central base, first night, real luggage: take the fixed-fare taxi and don’t feel fleeced.
d03.rest: The €55 buys door-to-door delivery on the trip’s most fragile day, and split two-to-four ways it’s competitive with the train once you count the onward hop. Take the Leonardo Express if you’re near Termini, travelling light, or solo — then it’s the clear winner. The FL1 is for the handful sleeping by its stations.

d04.title: How do you fit the ancient core into a day?
d04.strong: Give the ancient core its own half-day, and start with the Forum at opening.
d04.rest: Enter the Forum and Palatine when they’re cool and empty, break for lunch, take a midday Colosseum slot for the interior shade, and do not — whatever the ticket page tempts you toward — bolt the Vatican onto the same afternoon. Book the Standard combined ticket; the arena-floor upgrade is a separate decision with a separate deadline.

d05.title: What does “skip the line” actually skip at the Vatican?
d05.strong: Book the official timed ticket for the Museums; for St Peter’s, buy nothing and go early.
d05.rest: The Museums’ official slot is the real value and skips the only line a ticket can. St Peter’s basic entry is free, and the line is security. The museum-passage tour, opening/late-afternoon timing, and the official reservation with digital audioguide can each route you through faster — but everyone still clears security, and none of them is a purchased skip of the check itself. The Borghese’s mandatory reservation is your “skip the line” already. Pay a premium only for a guide you actually want.

d06.title: What must you book in advance — and how far?
d06.strong: Book the three that sell out the moment your dates are firm; leave the rest to the trip week.
d06.rest: The Vatican Museums, the Borghese, and — if you want it — the Colosseum's arena floor vanish fastest — check the official page for its current release window (recently about a week out) and reserve the moment it opens. The standard Colosseum and the Pantheon need only a day or two. Basic entry to St Peter’s needs no booking; the official reservation/audioguide service is a real product if you want it, not a requirement. Steer clear of the first Sunday unless the free entry truly matters more than the morning.

d07.title: Cards or cash — and the one prompt that quietly overcharges you?
d07.strong: Choose euros at every machine, tip like a local, and carry a little cash.
d07.rest: The dollars-or-euros prompt is the one recurring overcharge you control completely — always euros, always a no-fee card if you have one, always a bank ATM. Tip by rounding up, not by American percentage; the coperto isn’t a tip. Keep a day or two’s cash for small trattorias and tips, and no more — large sums are only pickpocket bait.

d08.title: How do you avoid eating badly in a city this good at food?
d08.strong: Don’t collect restaurant names; walk ninety seconds off the sight.
d08.rest: The trap density is highest exactly where the frontage is most valuable — facing the monuments — so the reliable move is to leave that frontage. Two or three streets back, look for a short Italian menu of Roman classics and a room that fills with locals after 8:30. That rule finds you a good meal almost anywhere in the core, and it never goes out of date.

d09.title: If you have a fourth day, where does it go?
d09.strong: For a single spare day, take Ostia Antica; save Pompeii for a trip that can spare a whole day to it.
d09.rest: Ostia delivers the ancient-port experience — real streets, real mosaics, everyday Roman life — half an hour out on a metro ticket, and leaves you an evening in Rome. Pompeii is the greater site and demands twelve hours and an early start; it rewards the trip that has the day to give, not the one squeezing in a fourth.
